newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's Tung names top judge and wins acclaim.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Tung names top judge and wins acclaim.

text.p: Hong Kong's future government named a reform-minded lawyer as its top judge on Tuesday in a decision hailed as strengthening chances of keeping the judiciary independent under Chinese rule.
The choice of distinguished barrister Andrew Li, 48, was announced by prospective leader Tung Chee-hwa whose plan to curb civil liberties has aroused Western concern.
Democracy campaigners hailed the choice of Li, an adviser to departing British Governor Chris Patten, to head a top appeals court, the last recourse to justice after China takes over in July.
The new Hong Kong court, based on a Sino-British agreement, will replace Britain's Privy Council on July 1 as the highest court for Hong Kong's 6.4 million residents.
Li, a member of Patten's advisory Executive Council, was described by one lawyer as "no puppet" and a legalist with a reformist streak.
The Cambridge-educated, Hong Kong-born Chinese lawyer will occupy a "hot seat" as Chief Justice of the Court of Final Appeal, on recommendations from a judicial commission.
At the same time, a visit by Chinese dissident and 1989 Tiananmen protest leader Chai Ling fanned up fresh controversy with China just weeks before the July 1 sovereignty change.

On Monday, the self-exiled Chai voiced concern about Hong Kong's future freedoms and urged the People's Liberation Army (PLA), whose second advance garrison party arrived in Hong Kong on the same day, not to repeat the army's crackdown on the 1989 democracy movement in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Chai, 28, who lives in the United States, arrived in Hong Kong last weekend on a one-week visa.
She said Hong Kong might set a democratic example to China in the future, and spoke in favour of political reform in her country, to which she hoped eventually to return.
China's mission in Hong Kong, the Xinhua News Agency branch, denounced Hong Kong authorities for allowing the territory to become a "base for subversion" against China.
In separate developments Britain said its new Prime Minister Tony Blair was considering a trip to Hong Kong to attend the grand handover ceremony at midnight on June 30.
And British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook lobbied Washington for support to ensure China sticks to its post-handover pledge of preserving Hong Kong's civil rights and financial freedoms.

"We will be looking for United States support to make sure that those agreements with China are honoured," Cook said after talks with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who plans to attend the handover ceremony.
Patten hailed Li's appointment, calling him a "very good lawyer" and a "most distinguished servant of Hong Kong". "It's very good news for the rule of law in Hong Kong," Patten said.
Hong Kong also welcomed news that U.S. President Clinton had decided to renew "most favoured nation" trade status for China, a perk that in turn helps buoy Hong Kong's external trade.
"We are grateful to know the President has taken Hong Kong's interests into account," said Trade Secretary Denise Yue.
The pace of change is quickening with only 42 days left until the historic end of Britain's empire in Asia.
Future leader Tung Chee-hwa, chosen by a China-controlled committee in December, has already shaped a handover government.
The naming of Li on Tuesday was the last major personnel move awaited to round off the post-colonial establishment.
Tung has retained 23 of the colonial administration's policy secretaries, roughly equivalent to ministers, including the highly popular Chief Secretary Anson Chan.
But he has picked a largely new Executive Council, mainly made up of pro-China business figures lukewarm on democracy.
The handover establishment also includes a solidly pro-China "provisional legislature" appointed by Beijing to replace the elected Legislative Council until fresh polls in 1998.
In Beijing, China dealt a new blow to rival Taiwan by barring Taipei's diplomatic allies from the future Hong Kong.
"It's impossible for countries that do not have diplomatic relations with China to maintain consulates in Hong Kong after July 1," said Foreign Ministery spokesman Shen Guofang.
China and Taiwan have been rivals since the Communists drove the Nationalists into exile on the island in 1949.
